name: Scalp cooling cap
lead: A scalp cooling cap is a tight-fitting cap that lowers scalp temperature during chemotherapy, with the aim of reducing chemotherapy-induced hair loss. Caps are either manual gel or ice caps that are frozen beforehand and swapped during treatment, or machine-based systems in which a control unit keeps coolant circulating [1].

The approach is used mainly by people with cancer rather than in looksmaxxing circles, and its relevance to appearance is the preservation of existing hair during hair-loss-inducing treatment. Randomized and prospective studies in women receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer have examined whether a cooling device reduces hair loss [2][3], and systematic reviews have pooled the wider literature [4][5].

Wikipedia notes that the procedure is likely to be useful with taxane or anthracycline regimens, that side effects are generally minor, and that caps are not advised where cancer is present in the scalp skin or in lymphoma or leukemia [1]. Costs in the US are described as roughly $1,500 to $3,000 per course [1].
infobox: Cooling cap (manual cold cap or machine-cooled system)

paras: Caps are usually made of neoprene, silicone or polyurethane and filled with gel or ice. Manual caps are frozen to roughly -25 to -30 degrees C before use, while machine systems use a control unit to keep the cap cold [1]. The terms cold cap and scalp cooling are often used interchangeably [1].

The first US patent, filed in 1979 and granted in 1984, covered Mark Barron's Chemo Cap, which used frozen gel-filled nylon pouches. Studies from the 1980s and early 1990s were discouraging, and the patent expired in 1998 [1]. A later review of 53 publications covered efficacy, side effects and controversies of scalp cooling [4], and an analysis of studies from 1995 to 2003 reported an average success rate of 73 percent in preventing chemotherapy-related hair loss [1].

Controlled evidence grew in the 2010s. A Dutch registry reported hair preservation outcomes and patient characteristics in 1,411 chemotherapy patients [6], and two papers published in JAMA in 2017 reported a randomized trial and a prospective cohort of a scalp cooling device in women with breast cancer [2][3].

Cooling the scalp is thought to constrict blood vessels and reduce how much chemotherapy drug reaches hair follicles, and to lower follicle metabolic activity. Reviews of the pathobiology of chemotherapy-induced alopecia describe it as typically acute diffuse hair loss with variable incidence and severity depending on the chemotherapy protocol [7].

Reported success varies with the chemotherapy regimen and other factors. A study of influencing factors examined characteristics associated with how well scalp cooling works [8], and a systematic review and meta-analysis assessed interventions for preventing chemotherapy-induced alopecia [5]. Earlier work described a system designed to effectively prevent such hair loss [9], and a systematic review of nonpharmacologic strategies for common chemotherapy adverse effects also addressed the topic [10].

Wikipedia describes side effects in chemotherapy patients as generally minor and says caps should not be used when cancer is present in scalp skin, or in people with lymphoma or leukemia [1]. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether scalp cooling during adjuvant or neoadjuvant breast cancer chemotherapy affects the risk of scalp metastases [11].

The SCALP randomized clinical trial and a companion prospective cohort study, both published in JAMA in 2017, assessed a scalp cooling device in women receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer and monitored adverse effects and quality of life [2][3]. The Dutch Scalp Cooling Registry described outcomes in 1,411 patients [6], and systematic reviews and meta-analyses have pooled results on hair preservation and on scalp metastasis [5][11].

Registered trials include a comparison of a scalp cooling system with a chemical cold cap in primary breast cancer (COHAIR) [13] and a small study of chemotherapy alopecia reduction in breast cancer [12].

card.summary: A cap that chills the scalp during chemotherapy to reduce hair loss; studied mainly in breast cancer patients, with trial support for that use.
card.aka: Cold cap, hypothermia cap, scalp cooling system
card.note: Studied for chemotherapy-induced hair loss, not general hair loss; not advised with scalp cancer, lymphoma or leukemia.

quick.overview:
A scalp cooling cap lowers scalp temperature during chemotherapy to reduce hair loss. It comes as frozen gel caps or as machine-cooled systems.

It is evaluated mostly in breast cancer patients, including a randomized trial and cohort study published in JAMA in 2017, plus registries and systematic reviews.
quick.mechanism: Cooling is thought to reduce blood flow and drug exposure at the hair follicle and slow follicle activity while chemotherapy circulates.
quick.risks: Side effects are described as generally minor. Caps are not advised where cancer is in the scalp skin or in lymphoma or leukemia, and a meta-analysis has examined scalp metastasis risk. US costs are roughly $1,500 to $3,000 per course.
